solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

blocks.note: first meaning: a friar of a Franciscan order known for its pointed hood
second meaning: a small South American monkey named after that hood

explanation.walkthrough: A primate is also a senior archbishop, so the surface reads as one churchman described twice; really the second half is the monkey.
explanation.definitionFit: The friar order and the monkey share a name, the monkey's cap of dark hair resembling the friars' cowl.

blocks.note: cha (or char) is informal British for tea
gall is bile, proverbially bitter

explanation.surface: A painter's favourite tipple turns out to taste unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'has': the artist has the drink followed by something bitter.
explanation.definitionFit: Marc Chagall was a Russian-French painter famous for dreamlike village scenes and stained glass.

blocks.note: first meaning: in law, a person who shares an interest in a matter or deed
second meaning: a toilet, 'john' being American slang for one

explanation.surface: Someone throws a celebration in honour of a man called John.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A party' reads as a celebration and 'John' as a man's name; both are nouns in other senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal usage calls a participant in a contract a privy, and an outdoor lavatory is also called this.

blocks.note: first meaning: a fenced enclosure within a jail or camp
second meaning: made of several parts

explanation.surface: A wing or block within a large prison complex.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase, 'prison complex' is a set of buildings; the break falls between 'prison' and 'complex'.
explanation.definitionFit: An enclosed yard in a jail bears this name, and something built from several elements is described the same way.

blocks.note: first meaning: as well, in addition
second, cryptic meaning: being 'into' something is being keen on it, and a good deal is a profitable buy

explanation.surface: Someone is excessively eager to make money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too keen' looks like one phrase meaning over-eager; instead 'Too' stands alone and 'keen on profit' is read literally as a playful paraphrase of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means 'as well, additionally', exactly what the adverb 'also' or 'too' conveys.

clue.text: For this reason, see guards left alone

indicators.note: a guard surrounds what it protects, so the earlier letters close around another piece

blocks.note: 'so' means therefore
a see is a bishop's diocese, and Ely is the classic crossword one
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A reason why someone watches over a person left on their own.
explanation.walkthrough: The two opening pieces together do the guarding, with the left letter placed where they meet. A see is a bishop's diocese; Ely in Cambridgeshire is the setters' favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean 'only, with nothing else involved', as in 'done solely by him'.

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one piece is placed round another

blocks.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of books
B is the abbreviation for British
use is the operation or working of something

explanation.surface: Heavy volumes about a British military operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thick' looks like a description of the books; it is the definition, meaning stupid.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe someone slow to understand, dull-witted or stupid.

clue.text: Polish drink served up with salt

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading the letters from bottom to top

blocks.note: ale is beer
a borate is a salt of boric acid

explanation.surface: Vodka poured with a pinch of salt, a Polish drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' with its capital looks like the nationality; it is the verb polish, to refine.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish a plan or text is to work it up in greater detail, to refine and develop it.

clue.text: Talk about dust marks in veil

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so the first piece goes round the others

blocks.note: to yak is to chatter
ash is fine dust left by burning
M is the abbreviation for the German mark, the old currency

explanation.surface: Someone discusses the dust marks left on a veil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'marks' is the old German currency, not stains; the chatter word is split after its first letter to take the others.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the double veil worn by some Muslim women in public, covering the face below the eyes.

clue.text: Inept toff replaced in Lords since when?

indicators.note: things replaced are put in new places, so the letters take new positions

blocks.note: the fourteen letters used as they are printed

explanation.surface: An incompetent aristocrat was replaced in the House of Lords, and someone asks since when.
explanation.walkthrough: A toff is a British upper-class person; the House of Lords makes the aristocratic surface natural.
explanation.definitionFit: This British phrase mocks an ineffectual upper-class man, the weak chin standing for weak character.

clue.text: Man wants a kiss first as a rule

indicators.note: coming first means going at the front, so these pieces precede the other one

blocks.note: taken as written
X is the kiss at the end of a letter
IOM is the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A man insists on a kiss before anything else, as a matter of principle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' puts A and X ahead of IOM. 'Man' is not a person but the island in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: An axiom is a basic principle accepted as true, a rule taken as given.

clue.text: Gauguin subjects I see in paintings

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it is placed inside

blocks.note: 'Ah!' is what you say when you realise something
Titians are paintings by the Venetian master Titian

explanation.surface: Someone recognises Gauguin's usual subjects in some pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I see' is an exclamation of understanding, not I plus a letter. It goes after the first letter of TITIANS.
explanation.definitionFit: Gauguin moved to Tahiti and painted its islanders, who became his best-known subjects.

blocks.note: surface reading: an option someone takes in extremity
setter's reading: rearrange the letters of these two words, as if tossed about by rough weather, and you get the first two words of the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone facing a desperate choice is told not to pray.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase describes itself: its first two words, whipped around by a tempest, become 'Pray not'. It is a reverse clue, so the wordplay is in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says that in trouble you accept whatever refuge or option is available, however poor.

clue.text: Hollywood location fails to secure investor

indicators.note: securing something means holding it fast, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: to fail in a contest is to lose
an angel is a backer, especially of a theatre production

explanation.surface: A film studio fails to attract a financial backer.
explanation.walkthrough: Angel is the theatre term for someone who puts money into a show, apt next to Hollywood.
explanation.definitionFit: Hollywood is a district within this Californian city, so the city is where it lies.

blocks.note: to sup is to drink, to down
a model's work is posing

explanation.surface: If someone is feeling down, they should behave as a model person would.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down' reads as sad, but it is the verb to down a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Both introduce a hypothetical condition: 'supposing it rains' means 'if it rains'.

blocks.note: first meaning: from an earlier time
second meaning: to support or stand up for

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a former title-holder; 'champion' is really a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Old numbers of a magazine are called back issues, and to support a cause is to back it.

clue.text: Gas, even a bit reduced, just delivered

indicators.note: something reduced is made shorter, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: neon is a noble gas
'at all' means even slightly, as in 'if at all'

explanation.surface: A gas supply, slightly cut back, has just arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'even a bit' is one phrase meaning in the slightest degree; it loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a newborn baby, one that has only just been born.

indicators.note: to tour is to go round, so one piece circles the other

blocks.note: 'as' means when, as in 'as I left'
an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: A band's album reaches the top of the charts while they are on tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peaks' looks like chart success; it is the mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps are the great European mountain range, a collection of high peaks.

blocks.note: a bow is a curve, an arch
a way is a road

explanation.surface: Bow Road is a real station on the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow Road is itself a London Tube station, so the clue looks like a plain name; Bow and Road are separate words to translate.
explanation.definitionFit: Archway is a station on the Northern line of the London Underground, known as the Tube.

clue.text: Musical tenor quits old form of Islam

blocks.note: Cats is the Andrew Lloyd Webber musical
T is the abbreviation for tenor
being quits with someone is being evens, all square

explanation.surface: A musical's tenor leaves an older branch of Islam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quits' looks like a verb, leaving; it means square. The singer took the name Yusuf Islam in 1977, so his old name is an old form of Islam.
explanation.definitionFit: The folk singer converted and became Yusuf Islam, so his earlier stage name is the former version of Islam.

indicators.note: in a down entry, a supporting piece sits underneath, so it comes second

blocks.note: steep can mean high, as in steep prices
le is 'the' in French, spoken in Nice

explanation.surface: A pleasant item holds up a tall tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' is the French city, not pleasant, so its article is French.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeple is a church tower topped with a spire.

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it is placed inside

blocks.note: L stands for the pound, from Latin libra
L is fifty in Roman numerals
a bank is a tier or row, as in a bank of seats

explanation.surface: A farm worker has fifty pounds deposited in the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bank' suggests money, but it is a row; and '£50' gives two separate Ls.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiller is one who tills the soil, cultivating land as a ploughman does.

clue.text: Event allowing seconds to be flogged?

indicators.note: something flogged is beaten about, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: the fifteen letters used as they are printed

explanation.surface: A shop event where cut-price imperfect goods can be sold off.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also reads as a description: seconds are flawed goods and 'flogged' is British slang for sold, so the anagram doubles as a hint to the event.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop shutting for good holds this sale as an event to clear its remaining stock cheaply.

blocks.note: 'Can I…?' asking permission is rephrased as 'Am I…?'
taken as written
a go is a start, as in 'we are go'

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they may begin working in China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can I start?' rephrases as the launch-control question 'Am I go?'. China is rhyming slang: china plate means mate, a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish word for friend, used in English too, matches china, which is British slang for a mate.

blocks.note: having a stab at something is giving it a whirl, an attempt
to snake is to wind, twist and turn

explanation.surface: Someone rashly knifes a snake on impulse.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'Stab' and 'snake' look like a violent verb and a noun; really a noun for an attempt and a verb for twisting.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adjective, as in a whirlwind romance, it means sudden and rushed, done on impulse.

indicators.note: to organise is to arrange, so the letters are set in a fresh order

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Wally has his wife along on a package holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Wally is British slang for a fool, not a man's name. The W joins the trip letters before they are mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Twirp, a variant spelling of twerp, is a silly or annoying person, exactly the British insult wally.

clue.text: Run back into tent for milk product

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters are read right to left
putting something into another thing places it inside

blocks.note: to run is to go
a yurt is a round Central Asian tent

explanation.surface: Someone dashes back into the tent to fetch a dairy item.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed pair lands after the first letter of the tent.
explanation.definitionFit: It is milk fermented by bacteria until thick and tangy, a dairy food.

clue.text: Writer, online bully, not quite honest

indicators.note: something not quite complete falls just short, so the last letter is lost

blocks.note: a troll posts abuse online
open means frank and honest

explanation.surface: An author who harasses people online is somewhat dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite honest' reads as shifty, but it only trims the word for honest.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope was a Victorian novelist, author of the Barsetshire novels.
